findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, including every ID in each batch.
findings.body: Each batch of every cleanup cycle logs two `r.log.Error` lines, and one of them includes the full `ids` slice. That slice can hold up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries; the new test uses 32767. With the ticker now at one minute, healthy installations will see a steady stream of false error logs, possibly with tens of thousands of IDs per line. That fills logs and can trigger error-based alerting. The same pattern appears at lines 554/557 and 576/579. Remove these lines, or move them to Debug and log only the count. The `err` value logged after `fetchIDs` is always nil at that point anyway.

findings.title: All cleanup jobs now run every minute instead of every 10 minutes.
findings.body: This change is about the MySQL deadlock in annotation cleanup. Changing the shared `CleanUpService` ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute also makes every other cleanup job run 10 times as often: temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, expired user invites, short URLs, and so on. That means more database load on every installation, and the request does not cover it. Revert to `time.Minute * 10`. If annotations really need a shorter interval, give them their own interval or setting.

findings.title: One placeholder per ID can exceed the bind-parameter limit on Postgres and MySQL.
findings.body: Before this change, the DELETE statements had no bind parameters, so any batch size worked. Now every database except SQLite gets one `?` per ID. Postgres and MySQL both cap a single statement at 65535 parameters. If `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` is set above 65535 on those databases, every cleanup DELETE fails and annotations stop being cleaned. Use the inlined integer list for any batch size above a safe limit on every database, since the IDs are int64 values read from the database and safe to inline. Alternatively, split `ids` into chunks of the parameter limit.
